items.definition: How far ahead the decision can see, which decides how urgent it feels.
items.example: Our decision horizons are different lengths, and that is the disagreement.

items.definition: The timing of the people around you, used as a reference point for your own.
items.example: Peer timing says everybody my age is married; peer timing is not a measurement of me.

items.definition: The pressure a family puts on the timing of its members.
items.example: Family pressure asks about grandchildren at the table, and the answer is a plan.

items.definition: A file sent together with the email. It should be named clearly and referred to in the body.
items.example: Please find the attachment, called Quotation-March-2026.pdf.

items.definition: The set of assumptions a person carries about how other people answer when they reach out.
items.example: My working model says that people get busy and come back, so I wait.

items.definition: The person or relationship a person can move away from and still feel steady in.
items.example: His sister was his secure base long before he had a partner of his own.

items.definition: The event that makes a person read a partner as less available than the person assumed.
items.example: One missed call was the trigger, and the rest of the evening went into reading the silence.

items.definition: Describing a person who takes the partner's availability for granted and stays steady when it wobbles.
items.example: She is secure with him, so she says she is upset instead of guessing.

items.definition: Describing a person who reads any drop in a partner's availability as a sign that the bond is at risk.
items.example: When he was busy, his anxious side read the quiet as a message about him.

items.definition: Describing a person who leans away when closeness increases, to protect independence.
items.example: His avoidant side called for less contact at the moment he needed it most.

items.definition: Describing a person who wants closeness and is afraid of it at the same time.
items.example: Fearful-avoidant behaviour often looks like pulling back right after reaching out.

items.definition: The rising of the alarm when a partner seems unavailable, which sharpens attention and speeds the urge to act.
items.example: Hyperactivation turned three unanswered messages into an hour of checking the phone.

items.definition: The lowering of the alarm when closeness increases, which turns attention away from the bond and towards the task in front of it.
items.example: Deactivation looked like a tidy desk and a long shift at the office.

items.definition: Asking a partner repeatedly to confirm that the relationship is still there.
items.example: Reassurance-seeking is asking the same question until the answer changes.

items.definition: The behaviour a person uses to get a partner's attention back when they feel the bond is slipping.
items.example: Her protest behaviour was sending the message twice and then three times.

items.definition: Pulling back from a partner and reducing contact when closeness or conflict increases.
items.example: Withdrawal is answering with less, not more, when the other person asks for more.

items.definition: The capacity to feel safe in a relationship, learned later in life rather than carried in from earlier life.
items.example: Her earned security came from a relationship that stayed, after years of ones that did not.

items.definition: The capacity to stay in charge of your own reactions when the other person is difficult.
items.example: Her emotional maturity showed in the pause before she answered, not in the answer itself.

items.definition: The capacity to hold a reaction and choose when to act on it.
items.example: He used self-regulation to stay in the room instead of walking out.

items.definition: Reading what another person feels, and taking it seriously enough to act on it.
items.example: Her empathy showed in the question she asked instead of the advice she gave.

items.definition: The answer you owe for an act, to the people affected and to the law.
items.example: The mistake was hers, and the accountability was hers as well.

items.definition: The capacity to stay with a delay, a refusal or a mistake without making the other person pay for it.
items.example: Tolerance of frustration is what a good team leader buys with a calm answer on a Friday.

items.definition: The leaning towards acting before you have looked at what the act will do.
items.example: The message went out in impatience, and the impulsivity cost him the job.

items.definition: How strongly and how fast a person reacts to pressure; a tempo, not a character.
items.example: Her stress reactivity is high in meetings and low in front of a machine.

items.definition: The work of managing your own feelings and other people's feelings so that the situation keeps running.
items.example: Emotional labour is the invisible work of keeping a meeting calm.

items.definition: The feeling part of empathy: catching what the other person feels.
items.example: Affective empathy made her notice that the new engineer was frightened in the group.

items.definition: The thinking part of empathy: seeing the situation from the other person's side.
items.example: Cognitive empathy is what lets you guess that the deadline was the real problem.

items.definition: Stating your need, your limit or your disagreement without wrapping it in blame.
items.example: Assertiveness is saying the report is late and then saying what you need instead.

items.definition: The leaning that keeps the peace by not raising the issue at all.
items.example: Conflict avoidance kept the meeting pleasant and the problem on the table.

items.definition: A belief about a group that is applied to a person without looking at that person.
items.example: That sentence about men and women is a stereotype, and it settles nothing about the man in front of you.

items.definition: The part of the value ranges of two groups that lies on top of each other.
items.example: The overlap between the two groups is wide, so the average says very little about one person.

items.definition: The process of choosing a partner, from the first interest to the decision.
items.example: Mate selection was slow for her and quick for her brother.

items.definition: The pull towards somebody, felt before any thought about the future.
items.example: The attraction was immediate, and that was not the same as choosing.

items.definition: What a person says they want, before any particular person comes along.
items.example: My preference was somebody older; the person I chose was younger.

items.definition: A quality whose absence ends the possibility, as opposed to one that only lowers the score.
items.example: Dishonesty was the deal-breaker, and the rest were preferences.

items.definition: The difference in age between two partners, and the direction of that difference.
items.example: The age gap was four years, and she was the older one.

items.definition: The range of ages a person thinks of as suitable when choosing a partner.
items.example: Her age preference was wide, and the people she chose were not.

items.definition: A span with a lower and an upper bound, used here for the ages a person will consider.
items.example: Write your age range as two numbers, not as a feeling.

items.definition: The pattern in which partners tend to be similar to each other on age, schooling, place or work.
items.example: Assortative mating was visible in the town: the teachers married teachers.

items.definition: How close two people are in space and time, and how often they meet.
items.example: Proximity did the work: they shared a shift and a bus stop.
